newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Profit-taking dents Australian bond rate cut rally.
newsitem.headline: Profit-taking dents Australian bond rate cut rally.

text.p: *The Australian 10-year bond yield finished only modestly lower as profit-taking reversed the immediate plunge which followed Wednesday's 1/2 point rate cut by the RBA.
*Bill futures trade below new 5.0 percent cash rate.
The Australian 10-year bond yield finished only modestly lower as profit-taking reversed the immediate plunge which followed Wednesday's 1/2 point rate cut after by the Reserve Bank.
The move to 5.0 percent official cash rates had been factored in for some time and the decision to cut today proved the only surprise for the market.
The benchmark October 2007 bond flirted with last week's sub-6.40 percent low on the announcement, but the rally quickly evaporated as the market pondered whether this was the last cut.
However, bill futures remained close to the day's highs with the December contract ending at 95.08, equating to a cash rate of 4.92 percent and below the new official rate.
Westpac Banking Group is strongly recommending investors and borrowers alike that they direct activity to another rate cut being priced into the yield curve over the next month.

"A confident central bank, a resilient Australian dollar and only moderate growth reponse to current low rates, all point to a further reduction over the next quarter," said Westpac's General Manager Economic, Bill Evans.
"Accordingly we have raised the probability of a third rate cut in 1997 from 50 percent to 60 percent, and our base case is a cash rate of 4.5 percent by end October 1997," Evans said.
Other analysts felt that another easing was less likely, which would be the sixth since July 1996, unless there was a spectacular downturn in economic activity.

"There is still a large degree of monetary stimulus to work through the Australian economy and we can be confident the RBA will now be inclined to take a more "wait and see" approach," said Glenn Maguire, economist at Societe Generale Australia.

The RBA said the rate cut was based on the current inflation outlook and expected underlying inflation to remain below 2.0 percent going in 1998. It also said that wage pressure had subsided and that there was still scope for faster growth.
Today's data for June building approvals was seen another reason why the central bank had to act, showing a 4.5 percent fall and being flat in trend terms.

"Today's rate cut should help, but the industry is by no means assured of a strong upswing. Lower interest rates are fine, but job insecurity is still playing on the minds of consumers," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial.

The local market showed only a modest spread tightening to the U.S. by the close after failing to make a decisive test of last week's 25 basis point low. New Zealand bond outshone the bloc as the N.Z. dollar took heart from the resilient performance of the Australian dollar on the rate cut.
